event: VXE 489 fuselage flying with the 408 center wing (battery, drop payload) transitioned to VTOL landing and the two front lift motors did not start for a few seconds; the aircraft pitched nose down, lost about 100 ft, recovered and landed normally.
component: 408 CW VTOL avionics (VTOL AP board and VTOL AP interface board 107-107306)
failure_mode: Front lift motors drew almost no power while commanded to full throttle from about 8848 to 8850 s; signal or power path to both front ESCs failed upstream of the boom harness split. Exact mechanism on the board not confirmed.
contributing: Nylon screw 100-102984 holding brass ballast weight 107-102859 sheared, weight scarred the AP interface board and dislodged R32
408 CW was not inspected or RMA'd after an earlier hard landing (VIT2-193)
VTOL logs on the SD card were corrupted, so ESC level data was not available

evidence.quote: The front motors, 1 and 2, were making no power at 8848 when the rears turned on. Vtol current is very low while the front throttles are railed from 8848-8850.
Here is data from running both forward lift motor/ESC assys on the dyno. Both have similar responsiveness and performance to that of an Iron Bird motor/ESC assy.
The nylon screw (p/n: 100-102984) that fastens the ballast weight (p/n: 107-102859) to the red AP interface board broke free, likely due to vibration.
From our testing, the weight did not interfere with Servo lines 1 or 2. It also did not interfere with the Ethernet traces on T4 that I had suspected before.
Highly likely that problem occurred before the signals physically split apart from each other which would be on the VTOL avionics
Contrary Finding in Analysis: The observed Loss of Ethernet Connectivity occurs significantly after the pitch and roll events that cause altitude loss.

team_root_cause:
Two possibilities exist:
- Likely:
Quality or design issue: VTOL controller mass damping bar (brass bar) detached, causing shorts, and damaging the circuit board.
- Much less likely:
Simultaneous issue with both front Lift Motors/ESCs or chip hardware issue impacting only the front two.

would_settle_it.file: 408 CW VTOL AP board and interface board 107-107306
would_settle_it.what: Scope the SERVO1 and SERVO2 PWM outputs and front ESC supply on the bench while pitching and vibrating the board, to find what blocked the front motors
Recovered or decrypted VTOL logs showing ESC telemetry and PWM output for motors 1 and 2 at 8848 to 8852 s

reasoning: XCOMM data show both front motors commanded to full throttle but drawing almost no current while the rears ran, then recovering. Both front motor/ESC assemblies tested normal on the dyno, and a failure in two separate boom harnesses at once is unlikely, which points to the shared VTOL avionics in the 408 CW. A sheared ballast screw had let the brass weight scar the interface board, which is the team's likely cause, but bench tests could not show the weight interrupting the servo or Ethernet lines, so the exact mechanism stays open.
notes: Motor numbers come from ENG-3040 ('The front motors, 1 and 2') and Kurt Burian's 'motor 1, FL'. During dyno testing motor 2 (front right) from 408 was overrun at 95% throttle and failed; the team judged this unrelated. VA-1030 and VA-391 were canceled with no further work. Ethernet losses found in the logs did not line up in time with the pitch-down.

Solder ball missed by Technician prior to close out of RF Shield

event: A TIQUILA customer VXE30 (tail not given) showed visible wing flapping vibration twice during VTOL landing descents; flights were stopped and the aircraft flew normally the next day.
component: VTOL AP attitude (roll) control loop gains, interacting with stiffer newer wing, joiner and lift boom structure
failure_mode: Underdamped left/right lift power oscillation near 8 to 9 Hz during crosswind hover or pause on descent, exciting the wing structure
contributing: newer, stiffer wing assemblies (manufacturing process improvements)
lift boom and joiner tube combinations influence amplitude
light crosswind with yaw hold instead of weathervaning
pause during descent

evidence.quote: The power is oscillating between the right and left sides of the vehicle at a frequency of ~8.7 Hz. To me this indicates an issue with gains resulting in an underdamped system.
I plotted the PSD of the Gyro roll rate and saw a mode at 7.9-8.7Hz across all of the datasets that Jack provided me.
These investigations failed to find a single smoking gun. However, it seems that our stiffer wings and control system are prone to approaching resonance when faced with a crosswind.
The center wing from 300 produced completely smooth hover, suggesting this oscillation is a linked to the mechanical properties of our newer wings.
I agree that it does not appear to be a flight safety concern, but is a gain/clock speed issue that we should be able to sort out.

[07:16:08.694] vt lch abort request from gcs
[07:16:31.777] vt lnd now during vtol active

team_root_cause:
The landing drift occurred due to a software bug. If a “Land Immediately!” command is issued from the GCS during an active launch abort state, the aircraft will become stuck in an attitude update only mode. In this mode the aircraft will not update the horizontal position to maintain desired position.
The vehicle did not descend, during the aborted launch, due to receiving continuous pause commands sent to the aircraft from the GCS.
reasoning: The GCS debug log shows the launch abort at 07:16:08 and a Land Immediately during the active abort at 07:16:31, followed by over a hundred pause commands. Code review showed mclandTrigger returning early on the second RTL so position update mode was never restored, and the drift was recreated three times on a HIL and fixed with a patch. The failure to descend was due to the held pause commands.
notes: Both debug logs are under 300 KB; the crash log was read in full up to launch and the rest scanned with repeated status lines (landing override display, CMD PAUSE, RTL, version pings) filtered out. event: Tails 522 and 529 could not connect to the GCS during LM source inspection because their XCOMM boards were stuck in a boot loop; investigation became the systemic SD card corruption study.

failure_mode: SD card file system corruption; the XCOMM SD driver hangs in initialization (timeout handling leads to access violation and watchdog reset loop) so the board never finishes booting
contributing: SD driver initialization timeouts lock up the processor instead of failing gracefully

team_root_cause:
- SD Card became corrupted. There are many different reasons an SD Card can become corrupted. We know the SD card write operation occurs in blocks every few seconds, if a power event occurred mid-write it could have corrupted the data or the card may have been faulty from the factory.
- Code is stuck waiting for a SD Card read in its initialization routine
- Removing the corrupted SD Card allows boot to succeed.
- Voltage leakage while unpowered and in storage causes a stored bit to flip from 1 to 0 and results in file and file system corruption.

would_settle_it.what: storage history and card part numbers for each corrupted card, to test the unpowered storage theory
vendor failure analysis of the NAND (planned with SanDisk) to tell bit rot from a factory defect

A debugger showed the firmware stuck waiting on an SD card read in initialization, and FS2-1661 found the driver timeouts lock the processor. Why the cards corrupted is not settled: a power cycling test found no corruption, and storage leakage is favored but called not conclusive.
notes: Tail 522's XCOMM was only recovered by re-pushing the bootloader; the 522-specific SD removal test is not recorded, so 522 is assigned by the shared symptom. Board 5-5306 had a card that could not be reformatted. Similar cases on 508 and 525. The two rework PDFs have no extractable text. event: Aircraft 546 attempted to transition to VTOL for landing after a mission, lost about 350 to 420 ft in roughly 30 seconds, and crashed west of the landing zone; the aircraft was a total loss.
failure_mode: Rapid altitude loss during early VTOL landing while the VTOL AP was still in land state 2 (waiting for LZ proximity); cause unknown
contributing: VTOL SD card removed by the customer and lost, so no VTOL logs
VTOL AP board damaged and would not power up
Lift current about 20% lower than a reference landing with sustained high throttle
Forward motor held high throttle longer than typical during transition

evidence.quote: Summary So Far: Although a VTOL land abort was logged and initiated due to an attitude fault, the abort was most likely not the cause of the crash. While log message timestamps are not precise due to internal system latency, the abort likely occurred after, or during, the impact.

At the end of the XCOM data log the vehicle was in the state of waiting for proximity to the LZ. Neither the fixed wing autopilot nor the VTOL autopilot had advanced to the descension state. This means the vehicle should not have started descending.

Low Lift Power: Comparing data from an NCR flight indicates that during this landing the lift system consumed ~20% less current during landing than some SCO flight data. The current level is also sustained as is the sustained high throttle value.
@Pat Wells Don’t think there’s anything remaining from engineering to do then. The VTOL AP board is also damaged and will not power up.

team_view_in_comments: the abort was most likely not the cause of the crash

would_settle_it.what: The missing VTOL autopilot SD card from the 4/13 flight: VTOL logs for attitude, lift thrust and land state during the descent
XComm XCL00134 lift current, VTOL throttles and fault flags during the 30 seconds before impact

reasoning: XComm data show the vehicle lost altitude rapidly while neither autopilot had entered the descent state, with lower than typical lift current at sustained high throttle. The logged land abort and lift fault came after or during impact, and the 12V bus drop to the VTOL AP matches impact damage. Without VTOL logs the reason the aircraft descended cannot be identified, so the evidence does not get past the symptom.

event: On aircraft 426 during VTOL landing, the vehicle descended very slowly from altitude, drained the battery to about 12%, lost control near the ground and came to rest on a fence about 15 m from the landing site; no damage.
component: VTOL AP AGL altitude estimate (LRF range fusion and baro AGL offset)
failure_mode: Spurious LRF ranges taken during fixed-wing flight were fused into the AGL estimate, giving about a 200 ft offset, so the vehicle switched to the 3 ft/s slow descent about 200 ft too high
contributing: Degraded VTOL main battery with low starting charge
Position overshoot on transition in wind delayed the descent
Nudge commands moved the position setpoint over the fence

evidence.quote: This issue is resolved. The problem was identified and a software fix has been implemented. The laser range finder occasionally picks up spurious range measurements during fixed wing flight and  the VTOL INS incorporates this range data into its relative altitude estimates. The software has been updated to ignore any LRF range measurements made during fixed-wing flight.
- 200 ft offset error resulted in transition to 3 ft/s descent rate 200 ft higher above ground than intenede (compared to 7.5 ft/s before reaching ground level)
- Apparently degraded VTOL main battery put operators under additional pressure as AV neared the ground
This is a 2-line change to ensure that the baro agl offset is only calculated when in VTOL flight (i.e. not in fixed-wing when the vehicle is up and away).

team_root_cause: Spurious LRF measurements made during phases of flight in which they aren’t expected and used in INS estimates for AGL altitude. The AV then thinks it is much closer to the ground than it actually is. As a result, it enters the slow descent phase of VTOL landing too soon and a very slow descent from high altitude results. The battery on the vehicle appears somewhat degraded and the charge level was not high to begin with. The slow descent resulted in battery exaustion resulting in loss of attitude control near the fence on the ground.
reasoning: Log analysis found a 200 ft AGL offset that made the vehicle start the 3 ft/s final descent 200 ft too high, giving a long slow descent that exhausted a degraded battery. The offset came from spurious LRF ranges during fixed-wing flight being used in the AGL estimate. The fix to calculate the baro AGL offset only in VTOL flight reproduced the corruption in HIL and corrected it, with v426 listed among the field cases.
notes: FS2-1753 first described the cause as a barometric drop mismatch between baro AGL and LRF AGL; the final Root Cause and the FS2-1807 test work put it on spurious LRF updates corrupting the baro AGL offset. The FS2-1807 slides say the exact corruption mechanism is still future work.

event: About three minutes after launch on aircraft 439, the vehicle went into an automatic Low Energy RTB that the operator could not cancel, although the GCS showed 75% main battery and 70% HLB; the aircraft landed without damage.
component: Launch wizard battery model selection (default battery model loaded after a mid-wizard vehicle restart)
failure_mode: Vehicle was power cycled during the launch wizard and the wizard was not restarted, so the FWAP used a default battery model with much lower endurance and triggered a Low Energy RTB
contributing: Software silently falls back to a default battery model after reconnect
Operations manual had no caution to restart the wizard after a power cycle
XComm datalog missing from the AAR for the incident period

evidence.quote: On the last flight, during the pre-flight phase, the vehicle was restarted in the middle of the launch wizard. I believe this was probably to resolve a sensor calibration error. Once the vehicle reconnected the launch wizard was not restarted. Instead, the operator proceeded from the same page of the launch wizard.

This sequence results in the vehicle using an incorrect (default) battery model. The battery model is what the vehicle uses to calculate endurance. The battery model used by default has a severely reduced endurance. I’m guessing it’s a model of a really old battery that used to be used on a predecessor to the current VXE-30. This is the reason the vehicle activated a low battery RTB ~ 3 minutes into the flight.
I was able to recreate this issue in our HIL by following the same steps.
Awaiting shipment back to customer. No Fault found on this aircraft. No repairs or rework required.

team_root_cause: Launch wizard was not restarted after resetting the vehicle.
reasoning: The Low Energy RTB was traced in the FWAP code to RTB time versus battery endurance. The XComm event log shows the vehicle was reset during the launch wizard without restarting it, which leaves a default battery model with very low endurance, and the same steps reproduced the RTB on the HIL. The returned aircraft was found to have no fault.
notes: The roll fault in the logs is normal on VTOL transitions per engineering. Why the operator pause request was rejected was raised but not answered in the ticket. The customer link to "HLB errors" was later moved to VXEP-532. The RMA-247 induction PDF has no extracted text.

event: On fuel cell aircraft 523, the HLB kept discharging after launch on several flights and the aircraft reported failure to maintain altitude, so the operators landed early and paused flight operations.
component: Pitot air data calibration (airspeed zero)
failure_mode: Pitot zero calibrated with pressure applied, so indicated airspeed read low; the aircraft flew faster than commanded, used near dash power in cruise, and power demand exceeded fuel cell output, draining the HLB
contributing: Possible operator error applying pitot pressure during the shield step
Possible software delay between calibration command and application (tests found 0.5 to 1 s)
Launch wizard does not check calibration quality

evidence.quote: @Cameron Chapman apologies I had shared some IM’s with @Jason Scherer on the side but did not update this issue.  This looked to me like a bad airdata calibration.  The groundspeed is consistently well above the airspeed.  We saw something similar happen on AV477 (I linked that issue above also).  Unfortunately I don’t have TAS in the xcomm log and I don’t see a VTOL log with this, but unless it was an extremely hot day I suspect a bad airdata cal.

- 4/23/23: I charted the Throttle Vs Power curves from XCL00050 (original cruise motor) and XCL00052 (Spare cruise motor). The power draw is nearly the same. This tells us that the issue is not with the motor. I also charted throttle vs power curves from another vehicle. This standard vehicle is drawing nearly half the power as VXE-523 for the same throttle value. See slide number 8 and 9 here:  Vehicle Investigation VXEP-368 v523 Data for charts here: VXE-523 investigation data XCL00050.CSV

The fuel cell from V523’s AAR  seems to be working well.  I see good power output after takeoff with a reasonable stack voltage and fuel consumption.  I do not understand where the ‘reporting [of] battery current of “-10”’ is coming from in the vehicle software, but I do not see any indication of negative current in the fuel cell files.  I did see that the comparison of HLB voltage (as measured at the fuel cell) and the HLB state of charge seems to be very noisy, and perhaps scaled inaccurately?

@Pat Wells I got pulled into a few other tasks, but my investigation was leading me to believe that the air speed data was reporting lower than actual. I base this on the comparison with ground speed consistently higher, the motor throttle higher, the altitude is reported as commanded, and the vehicle is pitching down more significantly than normal. If the vehicle thinks it’s flying slow it will increase throttle to maintain the commanded altitude. But if it’s flying faster than it thinks, it will need to pitch down to maintain the same altitude.

For this particular bird, an updated air data calibration can be performed.  This will likely resolve the issue.  After the airdata cal is completed, pressure can be applied and the airspeed reading observed.  The sensor is expected to read above 60 knots for a good cal.  Both 477 and 523 read below 40 knots with pressure applied.

team_root_cause:
Pitot calibration errors caused the air vehicle to fly too fast, resulting in more thrust usage than typical.
Root cause of calibration errors is unclear.  Leading theory is operator error, software issue causing delay in calibration, or some combination of both.

would_settle_it.what: XComm event log timing of SEND AIRDATA CAL against the pitot pressure step, as done for AV477 in VXEP-292
Ground test after a fresh air data calibration to confirm airspeed reads above 60 knots with pressure applied

reasoning: The fuel cell output looked normal, and swapping the cruise motor did not change throttle versus power, so the fuel cell and forward motor were ruled out. Groundspeed was consistently above airspeed, with high throttle and nose-down pitch, which fits an airspeed reading too low after a bad pitot zero; the pitot check read below 40 knots against a 60 knot expectation. The resulting high cruise power exceeded fuel cell output and drained the HLB.
notes: The two CSV summaries hold only column lists and row counts (892 and 659 rows), no logger header lines. Why the calibration was bad (operator pressure during the shield step or software delay) was not settled here; the sister case VXEP-292 later concluded operator error as best guess. A Low Energy RTB applies in fuel cell configuration (VXEP-377).

Photos and notes of the cracked cell and reactor holder location and fracture appearance

event: VXE 545 lifted about 3 ft at launch, was underpowered and unstable, dipped the right wing and dragged the wing tip before the launch was aborted, with minor wing tip and payload housing damage.
component: lift ESC soft-start circuit MOSFETs Q20-Q23 (Q20 found shorted)
failure_mode: soft-start circuit stayed off (gate at 0 V), starving the motor of current so it made low thrust at low and mid throttle; one soft-start MOSFET (Q20) later failed drain-source short
contributing: launch wizard has no check that flags a lift motor drawing less current than expected
pre-flight launch wizard only exercised motors 1 and 3, and motor 3 drew less power than the others
ESC heat sinking and missing flyback protection noted as weaknesses of the old ESC design

evidence.quote: See plots in the ppt, It is interesting that motor 3 drew less power than the other 3 motors.
@Cameron Chapman While probing the 545 ESC I found that Soft-start circuit MOSFETs were shorted. Upon further investigation, it was found that Q20-one of 4 MOSFETs in parallel was shorted.
I have managed to replicate the issue on end-of-life ESC. The problem occurs when the soft-start circuit does not come ON.
Upon further investigation, we found that Q20 was shorted.
This fault was localized to position 3 ESC.
Root cause narrowed down to the soft-start circuit of the ESC assembly in position 3 (right rear).

team_root_cause: Soft-start circuit in theVXE545 position 3 VTOL ESC was permanently OFF (i.e.. MOSFETs Q20-Q23 Off). This was causing the motor to get less current and deliver lower force. With the Soft start function OFF, the bulk capacitors would be disconnected from the circuit. The motor would operate, but with considerably lower force, as noticed by the customer. [CC1] [CC2] [RB3] [CC4] These components could be have been defective from the manufacturer, or damaged from heat or transients. It is very difficult to determine the cause of damage to integrated circuits. We believe time spent further investig

would_settle_it.what: check R40, R41 and C12 connections and Q20-Q23 for why the soft-start gate stayed at 0 V (open resistor, solder defect, or MOSFET batch issue)

reasoning: Flight data showed motor 3 (right rear) drawing less power in the launch wizard and running near full throttle at launch. On the dyno the returned assembly (S/N C-S100345) made low force until PWM 1500; probing and thermal imaging found soft-start MOSFET Q20 shorted, and shorting the soft-start gate on a stock ESC reproduced the same force curve. Motor THD and phase balance were normal, so the fault sits in the position 3 ESC soft-start circuit; why the gate stayed off was not proven.
notes: An early theory of a potting-contaminated phase solder joint was tested and rejected. The original low-force behavior disappeared after the pair was separated and reassembled, and a later run showed lower torque across the PWM range, which slightly clouds the bench record. VXEP-198 (old date code FDMS86540 MOSFET batch) was linked as background, not shown to apply to this ESC. Customer reported the motor as original to the aircraft (22 flights, 14.1 h).

Root cause was found to be a reduction in GPS rate on the ublox receiver.
The differences between fixed-wing and vtol heading estimates are typically quite large (5-20+ degrees in the logs I looked at).
We have discovered a software issue where sometimes the GPS update rate to the VTOL autopilot is too low - 5hz vs. 10hz expected.
We also found some information on a ublox forum that indicates there may be an issue with the M8N where it automatically falls back to 5hz.

team_root_cause:
Created powerpoint here.  Overshoot for this flight appears to be caused in part by attitude estimation errors.  Pitch estimation error is ~10 degrees during approach transition when pitch up should arrest forward velocity.
Root cause was found to be a reduction in GPS rate on the ublox receiver.  See investigation here.

team_root_cause:
- Poor Mating caused the incident OCT 30th 
- Melted anti-spark is a clear indication that a bad mate was made on the main battery. 
- When inserting the anti-spark pin into the socket the initial mate sees 6ohm to limit the inrush current and then once fully mated the connection should be around 2mohms. event: On two full-endurance fuel cell flights of VXE 732 (13 and 14 Nov 2024) the fuel cell stopped producing power from fuel starvation while the software still showed fuel remaining; one glide landing and one normal VTOL landing.
component: D450 fuel cell internal mass flow meter (fuel plumbed in reverse direction, reverse calibration)
failure_mode: Directionally sensitive mass flow meter plumbed backwards under-reported fuel consumed by about 10.8 to 13.3 percent, so the tank ran dry while fuel was shown remaining
contributing: Loss of fuel cell power did not trigger the fuel cell shutdown alert or automatic low-energy RTB
Early production defect affecting about 80 fielded units

evidence.quote: Upon performance of the test, both systems exhibited errors greater than 10% in the measurement
System’s D4500509 & D4500510 delivered initially August 2023, are among known 80 units
affected by manufacturing defect from early production that affected the plumbing of the fuel
The error % from this test is approximately 2.7%, which is within acceptable accuracy tolerance and
Post flight it was determined that the cause of the fuel cell error was fuel starvation.

team_root_cause: The primary root cause determined to be a manufacturing defect in the fuel routing through a directionally sensitive mass flow meter.  While plumbed in the correct flow orientation, the mass flow meter is able to accurately report fuel consumed within a 5% error margin.  When fuel is plumbed in the incorrect (reverse) direction, the measured fuel flow rate can become inaccurate, resulting in the under-reporting of fuel consumed.  The degree of inaccuracy is a function of the ambient temperature and fuel temperature at the time of use but is generally 8% to 13% over the -20°C to 50°C operationa
reasoning: Bench fuel sweeps against a calibrated mass flow sensor showed both returned fuel cells under-measuring fuel by more than 10 percent, matching the in-flight shortfall, and teardown found the fuel plumbed in reverse through the direction-sensitive flow meter from an early production defect. After re-plumbing and recalibration the error dropped to 2.7 percent on a full-tank endurance test. That is direct measurement plus a fix that removed the error.
notes: The report header reads Incident Number VIT2-500 / VXEP-732, which appears to be a typo for VXEP-780. The report says the reverse calibration is the suspected mechanism and the full scope is still under a QA CAR. Serial to flight mapping conflicts: the report pairs the 13 Nov AAR with D4500509, while the operator in ENG-2984 says 13 Nov flew S/N 510 and 14 Nov S/N 509. D4500509 stack also failed during return testing and was re-stacked (separate finding). The ENG-2984 report copy is identical to the VXEP-780 copy.

event: On 6 Dec 2024 at Fort Carson, VXE 541 failed to transition to VTOL lift on landing, kept slowing in fixed-wing flight and glided into the ground.
component: AS150 power contact, center wing to HLB connector
failure_mode: HLB connector not fully seated: marginal contact (about 5.7 ohm) limited lift current to about 5 A versus about 180 A needed, so lift motors could not start and the landing aborted into a lift system fault
contributing: Known dimensional tolerance mismatch between center wing male pins and HLB female sockets (assembly predates dimensional sorting)
Possibly not enough force applied by the operator when seating the HLB
Solder flow found in the center wing HLB connector
Landing state machine in LAND_WAITTRANS could not abort safely

evidence.quote: The HLB battery connection was not fully connected due to a previously identified dimensional tolerance issue or not enough force was applied when seating the connector by the operator.
Contact resistance measured 5.7 ohms approximately
Note: Low Current levels ~5 Amps vs typical ~180 Amps
Lift system did not pull expected power during landing. Current levels remain under 5 amps until the end.
he found solder flow in the Hybrid Lift Battery connector on the center wing.

team_root_cause: Connector was loosely mated to the HLB from the CW.

would_settle_it.what: Measure the HLB female socket diameters and contact force to confirm whether the part or the seating was at fault

attachments_read: 29105_F-855-002 Rev B - Edge Autonomy Return Authorization (RMA) Customer Form (VXE541).pdf.md
reasoning: XCOMM logs show repeated low-power and power-difference lift faults during the landing, and VTOL and XCOMM data both show lift current under about 5 A against about 180 A expected, with HLB voltage dips to near zero. The investigation measured about 5.7 ohm through the connector and found the center wing pins undersize relative to the HLB sockets, and the FSR found solder flow in the center wing HLB connector. Bench tests found XCOMM and VTOL working, so the marginal HLB connection is the cause.
notes: Whether the initiator was the known pin/socket tolerance issue or operator seating force is left open by the report; I chose manufacturing_quality since the assembly predates dimensional sorting. A hardware engineer comment in FS2-3321 suggested a lift ESC problem, but later data and testing pointed to the connector. Material disposition calls for replacing the dual current sense board, noting its connector was suspected as the initial failure. Purchase order and quote attachments are commercial only.

FWAP sensors populate and respond to avionics movement. FWAP versions populate on xcomm throughput.

this one can be prioritized ahead of that overall effort since it crashed a plane.

Current draw agrees that front prop and vtol motors were not on during this time.
